title: Emotions and Moods
description: Precise words for how people feel, from quiet contentment to intense joy.

cards.meaning: Having or showing a gentle, slightly sad longing, often for something in the past.
examples: She gave a wistful smile as she looked through her old photographs.

cards.meaning: Extremely happy and excited, usually because of something good that has happened.
examples: The team was elated when the proposal was approved.

cards.meaning: A deep, quiet sadness that lasts, often without an obvious cause.
examples: A soft melancholy settled over the town once the festival had ended.

cards.meaning: Easily annoyed or made angry.
examples: Lack of sleep made him irritable all morning.

cards.meaning: Quietly satisfied and at peace with what you have.
examples: She was content with a simple life and a good book.

cards.meaning: Worried or nervous that something bad may happen.
examples: Many staff were apprehensive about the restructuring.

cards.meaning: Nervous and unable to relax.
examples: Everyone was on edge while we waited for the results.

cards.meaning: Extremely pleased and happy.
examples: My parents were over the moon when I passed my exams.

cards.meaning: Feeling sad and lacking energy.
examples: He has been in low spirits since his best friend moved away.

cards.meaning: Feeling intense happiness and excitement, often for a short time.
examples: The crowd was euphoric after the final whistle.

title: Workplace Communication
description: Everyday phrases for meetings, emails and teamwork in a professional setting.

cards.meaning: To make brief contact with someone to share an update.
examples: Let's touch base on Friday to review our progress.

cards.meaning: To take further action after an earlier contact or meeting.
examples: I will follow up with the client after the meeting.

cards.meaning: To include someone in a conversation or email thread so they stay informed.
examples: Please loop me in on any emails about the budget.

cards.meaning: Sharing the same understanding of a situation or plan.
examples: Before we start, let's make sure we are all on the same page.

cards.meaning: The time or energy a person has available to take on work.
examples: I'm afraid I don't have the bandwidth to lead another project this month.

cards.meaning: To return to a topic later.
examples: We can circle back to the pricing question next week.

cards.meaning: A specific task agreed during a meeting, usually with an owner and a deadline.
examples: Each action item should have a clear owner and due date.

cards.meaning: A person or group with an interest in, or affected by, an organisation or project.
examples: We interviewed key stakeholders before drafting the communication plan.

cards.meaning: Open and honest, with nothing important hidden.
examples: Management tried to be transparent about the reasons for the change.

cards.meaning: Brief but clear and complete.
examples: Keep your update concise; the director only has five minutes.

title: Academic Writing
description: Formal vocabulary that helps you argue, evaluate and support claims in essays and reports.

cards.meaning: To provide evidence that supports a claim.
examples: You need to substantiate this claim with recent data.

cards.meaning: To combine ideas from different sources into a single, coherent whole. (American spelling: synthesize)
examples: A strong literature review synthesises findings rather than listing them.

cards.meaning: Logical, well organised and easy to follow.
examples: Each paragraph should build a coherent argument.

cards.meaning: To use cautious language so that a claim is not stated too strongly.
examples: Researchers often hedge their conclusions with words such as 'may' and 'suggest'.

cards.meaning: Based on observation, experiment or experience rather than theory alone.
examples: The study provides empirical evidence for the effect.

cards.meaning: Considering or because of (new information).
examples: In light of these findings, the policy should be reviewed.

cards.meaning: Mostly; in many ways but not completely.
examples: The audit was, to a large extent, successful.

cards.meaning: Despite; without being prevented by.
examples: Notwithstanding its limitations, the study offers useful insights.

cards.meaning: An idea or statement that an argument is based on.
examples: The argument rests on the premise that staff read every memo.

cards.meaning: A detailed analysis and judgement of a work or idea; to give such an analysis.
examples: Write a critique of the survey design, noting its strengths and weaknesses.

title: The Art of Persuasion
description: Language for convincing others, building arguments and winning people over.

cards.meaning: So convincing or interesting that it holds your attention.
examples: She made a compelling case for flexible working hours.

cards.meaning: The art of persuasive speaking or writing; sometimes used negatively for language that sounds impressive but lacks substance.
examples: The speech relied more on rhetoric than on evidence.

cards.meaning: To persuade someone to support you or agree with you.
examples: Her honesty won over the sceptical audience.

cards.meaning: To try to persuade by focusing on a particular feeling, value or reason.
examples: The advertisement appeals to parents' desire to keep their children safe.

cards.meaning: To influence someone's opinion or decision.
examples: Personal stories can sway an audience more than statistics.

cards.meaning: An argument that opposes another argument.
examples: Address the strongest counterargument before you conclude.

cards.meaning: To admit, often reluctantly, that something is true.
examples: He conceded that the costs were higher than expected.

cards.meaning: To give reasons in support of something.
examples: The report makes a case for investing in staff training.

cards.meaning: Clear, logical and convincing.
examples: She presented a cogent argument for reform.

cards.meaning: To persuade someone to change their mind.
examples: It took an hour, but we finally talked him round.

title: Nature and the Seasons
description: Descriptive words for landscapes, plants and the turning of the year.

cards.meaning: Green with grass or growing plants.
examples: We drove through verdant hills covered in tea plantations.

cards.meaning: Marked with patches of light and shade, or spots of colour.
examples: We walked along a path dappled with sunlight.

cards.meaning: The leaves of a plant or tree, considered together.
examples: The autumn foliage turned the valley red and gold.

cards.meaning: To produce flowers; a flower or the state of flowering.
examples: The cherry trees bloom for only a few weeks each spring.

cards.meaning: To become dry, weak and shrunken.
examples: Without water, the plants began to wither.

cards.meaning: The day with the longest or shortest period of daylight in the year.
examples: The June solstice is the longest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere.

cards.meaning: Alive but temporarily inactive or not growing.
examples: Many trees remain dormant through the winter.

cards.meaning: Growing thickly, richly and healthily.
examples: The garden was lush after weeks of rain.

cards.meaning: One of the two times each year when day and night are roughly equal in length.
examples: At the equinox, day and night are roughly equal everywhere on Earth.

cards.meaning: Something new and refreshing that improves a situation.
examples: Her ideas were a breath of fresh air in a dull meeting.

title: Cities and Travel
description: Words and phrases for exploring places, planning journeys and describing cities.

cards.meaning: Full of busy, energetic activity.
examples: We explored a bustling night market in the old town.

cards.meaning: Far from popular or well-known places.
examples: They stayed in a quiet village off the beaten track.

cards.meaning: A planned route or schedule for a journey.
examples: Our itinerary includes three days in Melaka.

cards.meaning: A strong desire to travel.
examples: Her wanderlust took her across six continents.

cards.meaning: A short stop between parts of a journey, especially between flights.
examples: We had a four-hour layover in Doha.

cards.meaning: Including people and influences from many different countries and cultures.
examples: Kuala Lumpur is a cosmopolitan city with food from around the world.

cards.meaning: To begin a journey.
examples: We set off before sunrise to avoid the traffic.

cards.meaning: The uncontrolled spread of a city into the surrounding countryside.
examples: Urban sprawl has replaced much of the old farmland.

cards.meaning: A building or place that is easy to recognise and helps people know where they are.
examples: The twin towers are the city's most famous landmark.

cards.meaning: To travel from place to place.
examples: It is easy to get around the city by train.

title: Time and Patience
description: Expressions about timing, waiting and the passing of time.

cards.meaning: Just before it is too late.
examples: We submitted the report in the nick of time.

cards.meaning: Lasting for a very short time.
examples: We caught a fleeting glimpse of the eagle before it vanished.

cards.meaning: Lasting a very short time; more formal or poetic than 'brief'.
examples: Fame on social media is often ephemeral.

cards.meaning: To wait patiently for the right moment to act.
examples: She bided her time until a senior position became available.

cards.meaning: Lasting longer than expected or usual.
examples: The negotiations were protracted and exhausting.

cards.meaning: At the appropriate time; eventually.
examples: You will receive your results in due course.

cards.meaning: Continued effort to achieve something despite difficulty or delay.
examples: Learning a language well requires perseverance.

cards.meaning: Time seems to pass very quickly.
examples: Time flies when you enjoy your work.

cards.meaning: To wait for a short time; or to keep going in a difficult situation.
examples: Hold on, I'll check the schedule.

cards.meaning: The period between two events; temporary, for that period.
examples: In the interim, Sarah will manage the team.

title: Money and Value
description: Vocabulary for spending, saving and judging what something is worth.

cards.meaning: Careful with money and avoiding waste.
examples: Living frugally helped her save for a master's degree.

cards.meaning: Spending much more than is necessary or sensible.
examples: The launch party was extravagant for a small start-up.

cards.meaning: To have just enough money to pay for what you need.
examples: Many families struggle to make ends meet.

cards.meaning: Something that costs far more than it is worth.
examples: Twenty ringgit for a bottle of water is a rip-off.

cards.meaning: Wealthy; having plenty of money.
examples: They grew up in an affluent neighbourhood.

cards.meaning: Extremely useful. Note: it does not mean 'without value'.
examples: Her advice was invaluable during my first year at university.

cards.meaning: To spend a lot of money on something enjoyable.
examples: We splashed out on a nice dinner to celebrate.

cards.term: cost an arm and a leg
cards.meaning: To be very expensive.
examples: That new laptop cost an arm and a leg.

cards.meaning: To plan how you will spend money; a plan of income and spending.
examples: Students should budget carefully for the semester.

cards.meaning: Worth the time, money or effort spent.
examples: The extra training proved worthwhile.

title: Conflict and Resolution
description: Words for disagreements and the ways people settle them.

cards.meaning: A strained feeling between people or groups that may lead to conflict.
examples: There was tension between the two departments.

cards.meaning: To remove misunderstanding or bad feeling by talking openly.
examples: A frank conversation helped to clear the air.

cards.meaning: An agreement in which each side gives up something it wanted.
examples: After hours of discussion, they reached a compromise.

cards.meaning: To become more serious or intense.
examples: The disagreement escalated into a formal complaint.

cards.meaning: To help two opposing sides reach an agreement.
examples: HR was asked to mediate between the manager and her team.

cards.meaning: To end a quarrel and become friendly again.
examples: After years of rivalry, the two writers buried the hatchet.

cards.meaning: A complaint about being treated unfairly.
examples: Staff can raise a grievance through the official process.

cards.meaning: In disagreement or conflict.
examples: The two reports are at odds over the cause of the decline.

cards.meaning: To restore friendly relations; or to make two ideas fit together.
examples: They reconciled after a long silence.

cards.meaning: Opinions or interests shared by people who otherwise disagree.
examples: Despite their differences, they found common ground on safety.

title: Memory and Nostalgia
description: Language for remembering, forgetting and longing for the past.

cards.meaning: A sentimental longing for a happy time in the past.
examples: The old song filled her with nostalgia.

cards.meaning: To talk or think with pleasure about past experiences.
examples: We spent the evening reminiscing about our school days.

cards.meaning: Very clear, detailed and bright in the mind.
examples: I have a vivid memory of my first day at university.

cards.meaning: Unclear or vague.
examples: My memories of that trip are hazy.

cards.meaning: To sound familiar.
examples: The name rings a bell, but I can't remember where we met.

cards.term: on the tip of my tongue
cards.meaning: Almost remembered but not quite.
examples: His name is on the tip of my tongue.

cards.meaning: To honour and remember an important person or event.
examples: A plaque commemorates the founders of the school.

cards.meaning: Bringing strong images, memories or feelings to mind.
examples: The writer's descriptions of the coast are wonderfully evocative.

cards.meaning: To help someone remember something.
examples: Looking at the photos might jog your memory.

cards.meaning: Belonging to an earlier time.
examples: The film captures the charm of a bygone era.

title: Art and Creativity
description: Words for making things, finding inspiration and judging creative work.

cards.meaning: A person or thing that inspires an artist or writer.
examples: The sea was her muse for many years.

cards.meaning: A set of ideas about beauty or style; relating to beauty and appearance.
examples: The app has a clean, minimalist aesthetic.

cards.meaning: Placing two different things side by side to highlight the contrast between them.
examples: The juxtaposition of old and new buildings is striking.

cards.meaning: New, experimental and ahead of its time, especially in the arts.
examples: The gallery shows avant-garde work by young artists.

cards.meaning: To think creatively and in an original way.
examples: We need to think outside the box to solve this problem.

cards.meaning: An outstanding work of art; a person's best work.
examples: Many critics consider the novel her masterpiece.

cards.meaning: To create or perform something without preparation.
examples: When the slides failed, she improvised brilliantly.

cards.meaning: Copying the ideas of others too closely; not original.
examples: Critics found the album derivative and predictable.

cards.meaning: A natural talent for something; stylishness.
examples: He has a flair for graphic design.

cards.term: in the eye of the beholder
cards.meaning: From 'beauty is in the eye of the beholder': beauty is a matter of personal opinion.
examples: Whether the building is beautiful is in the eye of the beholder.

title: Food and Flavour
description: Descriptive words for taste, texture and the pleasure of eating.

cards.meaning: Salty or spicy rather than sweet. (American spelling: savory)
examples: I prefer savoury snacks to sweets.

cards.meaning: Having a sharp, pleasantly sour taste.
examples: The tangy tamarind sauce balanced the rich fish.

cards.meaning: Having a strong, pleasant smell.
examples: The curry was rich with aromatic spices such as star anise and cinnamon.

cards.meaning: Lacking strong flavour; dull.
examples: The soup was bland, so I added some chilli.

cards.meaning: Juicy and tender in a pleasant way.
examples: The grilled chicken was succulent and perfectly seasoned.

cards.meaning: A person's sense of taste.
examples: The tasting menu was designed to delight the palate.

cards.meaning: To make you want more of something.
examples: The trailer whetted my appetite for the film.

cards.meaning: Something very easy to do.
examples: The first quiz was a piece of cake.

cards.meaning: Good for your health; also morally good.
examples: She cooks simple, wholesome meals for her family.

cards.meaning: So tasty that you want to keep eating more.
examples: These crackers are dangerously moreish.

title: Technology and the Digital World
description: Vocabulary for devices, software and life online.

cards.meaning: No longer used because something newer has replaced it.
examples: Fax machines are almost obsolete in most offices.

cards.meaning: The newest and most advanced.
examples: The lab uses cutting-edge equipment.

cards.meaning: Easy for people to use or understand.
examples: The new portal is far more user-friendly than the old one.

cards.meaning: A small, sudden fault in a system or machine.
examples: A glitch in the system delayed payments for a day.

cards.meaning: To make a process simpler and more efficient.
examples: The software streamlines the approval process.

cards.meaning: To make a copy of data so it is not lost.
examples: Always back up your work before installing an update.

cards.meaning: The record of data a person leaves behind through their online activity.
examples: Be careful what you post; your digital footprint can last for years.

cards.meaning: To find and fix problems in a system.
examples: The IT team spent the morning troubleshooting the network.

cards.meaning: Easy to understand and use without instructions.
examples: The interface is so intuitive that no training is needed.

cards.meaning: To spread very quickly and widely online.
examples: Her video went viral overnight.

title: Health and Wellbeing
description: Words for looking after the body and mind.

cards.meaning: Physical and emotional exhaustion caused by long-term stress.
examples: Long hours led to burnout among the nurses.

cards.meaning: Involving a lot of sitting and little physical activity.
examples: A sedentary lifestyle increases several health risks.

cards.meaning: To recover from illness, injury or tiredness.
examples: He took a week off to recuperate after surgery.

cards.meaning: Treating the whole person or system, not just one part.
examples: The clinic takes a holistic approach to patient care.

cards.meaning: Slightly ill.
examples: I'm feeling a bit under the weather today.

cards.meaning: Able to recover quickly from difficulties.
examples: Children are often more resilient than adults expect.

cards.meaning: To relax after a period of work or stress.
examples: I unwind by walking in the park after work.

cards.meaning: In very good health.
examples: My grandfather is eighty and still fit as a fiddle.

cards.meaning: The habit of avoiding excess.
examples: Sweets are fine in moderation.

cards.meaning: Consciously aware of something; attentive to the present moment.
examples: Try to be mindful of your posture when you work at a desk.

title: Friendship and Loyalty
description: Language for close bonds, trust and the people who stand by us.

cards.meaning: A person you trust with private thoughts and secrets. (Often spelled 'confidante' for a woman.)
examples: She has been my confidante since primary school.

cards.meaning: Firm, loyal and unwavering.
examples: He remained a steadfast friend through difficult times.

cards.meaning: To like each other immediately.
examples: We hit it off on the first day of orientation.

cards.meaning: A friend who is only there when things are going well.
examples: When I lost my job, I learned who my fair-weather friends were.

cards.meaning: Mutual trust and friendship among people who spend a lot of time together.
examples: There was a strong camaraderie among the volunteers.

cards.meaning: To gradually become less close.
examples: We drifted apart after university.

cards.meaning: To support someone, especially in a difficult situation.
examples: Her friends stood by her throughout the crisis.

cards.meaning: A friendly relationship in which people understand each other well.
examples: A good lecturer builds rapport with students.

cards.meaning: Someone who listens and comforts you when you are upset.
examples: He was always there as a shoulder to cry on.

cards.meaning: To have known each other for a long time.
examples: Mei and I go back a long way.
